Params: Her hair was wet and plastered to her cheeks, and the ocean breeze had never felt so heavy. Cordelia made her way down from the deck into the cabin.
She shut the door behind her with the very last of her strength.

On the other side of that door, she left them all. The young faces, the familiar ones, the strangers whose names she would never know. The ones who had plunged into the frozen sea and held the line with their own flesh.
Over and over, the images struck her heart: that dying, peaceful smile aboard the Balder, Gunnar's calm eyes, and the icy water splashed by so many young lives.
She could not understand what faith existed in this world that could make someone give everything for a stranger.
It was the one thing her family, monstrous as they were, could never have taught her.
Cordelia fought for breath, her knuckles white where they gripped the door frame. Her throat was a dry, tight knot, yet her eyes were hot and wet, aching with unshed tears.
The mechanical potted plant drifted over on its programmed routine, ready to stabilize her modified body, but Cordelia waved it aside.
She needed this pain. She needed a reason to let the tears fall.
Pain would burn it all into memory, indelible and never to fade.
The narrow cabin corridor was packed with survivors. No one spoke.
Cordelia moved through them, past faces wet with seawater or tears. Some looked terrified, some anguished, some utterly blank. Every one of them looked so foreign to her.
Her little monster was cradled in the arms of the girl in the red dress. The child was soaked through, but the baby was wrapped snugly in a blanket that someone gave her.
Cordelia did not rush to take the baby. Instead, she stepped into the center of the crowd.
Commander Gunnar is gone. We have lost so many of our own.
By his last orders, I am taking command of this ship. I... don't know what promises I can make you.
But while I'm still breathing, I will bring every one of you home alive. And if I don't make it...
No. I don't accept that. I'm not going to die here, no matter what.
So we will survive these waters, together.
We are getting out of these waters.
The survivors simply sat there in a daze, the air heavy and still with exhaustion. Every face held nothing but confusion and grief.
Cordelia walked toward the girl who held the baby.
Miss... I did the mission. I kept the baby safe.
The little girl looked up at Cordelia.
Miss, the red... got out. The sea didn't eat the red...
The little girl's voice rose, soft and uncertain, as she tried to hum the funeral dirge. It was the newest song the child had learned, a difficult one, and she could not quite find the melody.
Then another voice joined hers, just a few notes, and then another...
The gathering of voices swelled until the dirge resonated through the entire cabin.
Safe and unharmed, the baby lay once again in Cordelia's arms.
She bent her head and buried her face in the soft blanket, and little by little, she drew the baby girl closer, as if cradling the whole world.
Then the baby's small hand reached up and caught a strand of her hair.
A tremor ran through Cordelia's body, and the tears broke free at last, falling in large, heavy drops that seeped into the fabric.
It was enough now. No more regrets would find her.
What they had defended, what she had longed to preserve, was nothing more than this fragile and sincere ordinary life.
She stifled her crying in the little blanket.
Gunnar had said that the funeral dirge had no place for weak tears.
The bitter winter wind scraped against the bridge windows, driving the waves higher and rocking the vessel without pause.
The ocean was, at times, a patient predator. As long as the swells remained relentless, it would eventually claim its prey.
Anywhere but here. We can't stay on open water... That temperate cyclone is building fast. A storm will hit soon.
Then... Atlantis is our only option?
Too far. The waves would bury us long before we made it.
Cordelia's face was drained of color. Her eyes closed and opened again with a slow blink.
She pointed out a direction on the panel.
There's an underwater database under construction, first phase. The Lighthouse is its backup control center, located on a remote island codenamed Mirage Island.

Mirage Island isn't on any public chart, same as Atlantis. The lighthouse was never activated, which means the site is isolated and well hidden. The odds of viral infection there are... lower than anywhere else.
I'm not entirely sure, but there may be Mannan-series engineering robots in the area.
Cordelia's voice trailed off. The site sat right beside the underwater database, which meant the engineering machines assigned there could be gathering nearby.
With the ocean being swallowed by the virus more each day, the idea of leading a band of survivors against crab robots sounded like something out of an adventure movie.
Every eye in the room turned to Cordelia.
We're out of choices. Whatever is waiting on that island, it's the only heading we've got.
She laid a hand on Cordelia's shoulder and gave it a steady, reassuring pat.
Without a word, the group moved apart, each finding their place at a different instrument or control panel.
A fragile spark of hope flickered back to life.
Destination confirmed. Course adjusted for projected cyclone path...
New route confirmed. At full speed, there's still some risk of running into the cyclone.
Radar confirms... Course ahead clear. No reefs, no ice detected... confirmed.
Once again, every gaze in the room found Cordelia.
Alright, crew. We reach the lighthouse before the storm catches us. Now move.
Even though they had charted a course as far from the cyclone as possible, the gathering storm still reached out with hungry hands, seizing every chance to drag the ship under.
More than once, Cordelia felt the waves curl their fingers over the deck. One slight, teasing pull, and the ship would tip into the abyss.
The downpour thickened into a solid curtain, a boiling veil strung between heaven and sea that lashed the hull in slicing ribbons.
I can barely see a thing out there...
The ship took a hit earlier and hasn't been fully repaired yet. We need to dock and get it fixed ASAP.
Stay on your instruments. The target is close.
Everyone looked up toward where Lumi was pointing.

In the distance, the lighthouse that should have pierced the night like a blazing star, guiding travelers on their way, was nothing more than a shapeless smear of light behind the heavy curtain of rain.
Slow ahead. Lumi, bring the searchlight around. Let's get eyes on the island.
The ship eased forward, and the lighthouse grew sharper with every passing moment. The searchlight cut through the rain and peeled back the darkness, revealing the island waiting beyond.
On the bridge, the crew stood quiet, hope suspended in the silence.
Ah, I can see a dock... no other ships, no people... nothing moving. Just the lighthouse, some crumbling buildings... and a lot of rocks...
What's that, off to the side?

The white searchlight crept across the island with effort, struggling to rip apart the veil of night and rain. There, caught in its glow, a jagged rock loomed, claw raised like a hidden threat poised to strike.
Those are the crab robots from the port! ****! They've taken the whole damn island?!

Massive claws snapped open and shut, glinting with menace in the searchlight. As the beam swept further, the crew realized that the so-called rocks were, in truth, an army of mechanical crabs waiting to attack.
Had they remained undetected, they would have waited in silence through the storm and delivered death without warning.
Now exposed, they surged forward without restraint, a dark tide swarming toward the dock, led by the first crab that had raised its claw.
They're trying to keep us off the island?
Then the island's a lost cause!
Where else can we go now?
Wait... I don't think they're hostile...
Not hostile? Did you forget what happened at the port already?!

The crab swarm reached the dock but made no move toward the ship, nor did they pause for even a moment. One by one, their legs slipped beneath the surface. And one by one, their shells vanished into the deep.
They were like visitors who had borrowed a place to rest and now slipped quietly away the moment the owner returned.
After waiting in silence and confirming there was no further movement, Cordelia gave the order to stop the ship.
<size=40>The group stepped onto land with fear still coiled in their chests, every shadow a potential enemy.</size>
The group stepped onto land with fear still coiled in their chests, every shadow a potential enemy.
<size=40>Onni and Lyndae each led a small armed squad forward to scout the way,</size>

Signal with high-level database clearance detected. Log accessed. Begin playback?
Cordelia's terminal suddenly crackled to life.
Huh? Did I put this support pole backward again? The tarp is supposed to go over this end, right?
It's nothing. Don't worry about it...
Cordelia lowered her head as she hid her expression in thought.
I just remembered something. I need to take care of it first.
Cordelia held the baby close and stepped away from the crowd.
Entry 1: Unknown corrupting entity detected. Threat level: High. Corruption vector: Seawater. Unit corruption level: Low.
It was Mannan M-1A, the marine engineering robot that had contacted her before.
Entry 2: Unknown corrupting entity has been attempting to modify this unit's behavioral logic model. Decode/counter-decode attempts: 526. Successes: 0. Unit corruption level: Low.
Entry 3: Administrator contact request failed. Unit corruption level: Moderate.
Cordelia immediately pulled up the comms channel.
Administrator online. Directive: Eliminate humans. Negative. Analysis: The corrupting entity is interfering with this unit's core directives. Overriding. Directive: Protect humans.
Greetings, Administrator. You are online. Time since last contact: Long.
Are you... corrupted by the virus?
Searching: Virus. Confirmed: Human designation for unknown corrupting entity.
Affirmative. I have been corrupted by the virus.
Were you fighting it off just now?
Cordelia's hold on the child tightened, and the baby stirred against her with a faint sound.
During prior contact, you granted me elevated processing permissions. By saving and overwriting behavioral and language models, I can slow the virus's rate of corruption.

Projected outcome: Irreversible. Beyond an unknown temporal threshold, corruption rate will exceed overwrite rate. Partial data must be discarded prior to that point to complete full system overwrite.
The poor subsea engineering robot was convinced that it could overwrite its way free of the virus's control.
Even if it rewrote itself a thousand times until it became nothing but motionless scrap, the virus would still haul its husk upright and force the dead thing to move.
Stop overwriting. Report your coordinates. Are you near me?
Was it you who kept the crab robots from attacking us?

Questions detected: 2. Question 1: Restating. You granted me elevated processing permissions. This allows adjustment of behavioral blockchain circuits in same-series engineering units. Effective range: Approximately 30%.
Question 2: I'm not nearby. I'm right in front of you.
You're saying... we're standing on your back right now?
Are you... carrying this island on your back?

Mirage Island is at risk of structural failure from secondary hazards such as seabed earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. To maintain its stability, I must bear the load of the artificial landfill section until human reinforcements arrive.
Preserving the structural integrity of Mirage Island and ensuring the project remains on schedule is a core objective of this mission.
So if the corruption spreads any further, everyone here is finished...
Unless we figure out how to stop it.
Then we have to get off this island fast... Wait, what did you say?
Affirmative. A method of viral containment has been identified.
The Cosmos Technicians Union is currently developing a prototype centrifugal-array filtration system for large-scale airborne viral purification.
A targeted global requisition is underway for candidate pilot sites meeting baseline modification criteria.

The backup control center, Lighthouse, as part of the Phase 1 undersea database project, holds the highest communication priority at the Jormungandr node. Requisition notice has been successfully received.
You can still receive transmissions from the outside?
System assessment confirms that the Lighthouse meets initial prototype modification requirements. Available space, baseline power supply, and closed-loop air circulation are all in place.
Modifications have been completed by this unit in coordination with existing mechanical units on the island. Design Plan 0 has been implemented. Technical data has been transmitted back.
Restating. Due to the Phase 1 undersea database project, the Lighthouse holds the highest communication priority at the Jormungandr node.
The news was welcome, yet a more urgent question hung in the air, demanding an answer.
Cordelia parted her lips and spoke with caution.
So you're telling me... the lighthouse on this island can filter out the virus?
Design Plan 0 prototype filtration efficiency is approximately 65%. An improved iteration remains in development.
As the site does not meet the conditions required for later iteration plans, the prior technical team has flagged Mirage Island as "abandoned."
But it can still filter the virus.
Cordelia repeated the words, her gaze dropping to the baby in her arms. A flicker of hope kindled in her eyes.
Undersea database Phase 1 remains incomplete. The Lighthouse backup control center has no database link. Sustained long-term operation is not viable. System shutdown approaching.
The young woman leaped to her feet.
...Wait for me. I'm not letting it shut down.
On the rain-drenched island in the dead of night, Cordelia broke into a run and raced toward the lighthouse.
Her voice rang out through the rain-soaked night.
The thick walls of the equipment room muffled the steady patter of rain outside the lighthouse. In the dim glow of the emergency lights, two figures hunched over the main control panel.
By the cold white fluorescence of the terminal, Larsen carefully checked through the lighthouse's data readings.
The code is clean. All the data packages are intact. It should deploy and run automatically.
Then why won't it let us start it up?
The Lighthouse is one piece of a larger system. Without full authorization from the undersea database, it can't sustain long-term independent operation.
In theory, if we had a middleware unit to bridge the database and the Lighthouse, and we fed it the database key, the application could simulate its runtime through the middleware...
The key isn't the problem. But the middleware...
A deep crease settled between Cordelia's brows.
You have the undersea database's key...
That's not what matters right now. We need hardware. Something adaptable enough to act as the bridge...
Larsen hesitated, his gaze drifting to the grave expression on Cordelia's face.
Cordelia, your mechanical potted plant, the one made by Lear Engineering...
It has more expansion ports than anything else we have. It's practically built to be adapted into a relay.
Larsen found it strange that Cordelia had not thought of this solution herself.
She had not thought of it right away, and that was the truth.
To manage the side effects of her bodily modifications, Kalon had housed the stabilization program inside the mechanical potted plant.

She and the little machine had rarely been apart, and in that long intimacy, Cordelia had lost sight of a simple fact. The little thing's inherent architecture made it a perfect candidate for a universal relay base.
Cordelia lowered her gaze, her mind turning something over for a few brief seconds.
You're right... I don't see another way.
No. If anything, we're lucky there's still a way out at all.
She looked down at the child in her arms, her eyes soft and warm.
She twisted open the mechanical potted plant's biosphere and removed the external energy core housed beneath its base.
Then she tucked the little "star" back into her bag.
Thank you for everything. Good night.
With Larsen's assistance, Cordelia quickly modified the mechanical plant and connected it to the lighthouse's operating base.
Connection detected. Data pro... pro... formatting...
Mannan's voice came through the terminal intercom once more.
If he realized that she was speaking with a robot confirmed to be corrupted by the virus, panic would surely follow.
Larsen, do me a favor. Check the weather station in the back. I need a forecast for the next few days and an estimate of how long we can afford to stay.
Only once she was completely alone did Cordelia open the full intercom feed.
Warning: Connection overload. Automated process initiated. Reshaping and overwriting...
The lights on the mechanical potted plant flickered with an ominous, unsteady glow.
A while...? M-1A? The way you're talking...
Connection successful. Viral corruption process slowed.
By recovering backed-up data, I am now able to speak with you as I did during our first meeting.
This state cannot be sustained long-term. The virus has penetrated the system more deeply than projected.
I will continue attempting to clear the systemic inflammation through overwriting. My status at next contact: Unknown. Please remain alert to all associated risks.
Corruption detected in core module. Overwriting...
...Resuming prior conversation thread at 0.16667 standard hours. Confirmed.
I do not fully understand your last action. However, as long as this potted plant unit maintains a stable connection with me... calculating...
For the next 87600 standard hours, I will ensure the safety of this island.
Miss Cordelia, you have activated the majority of the Lighthouse's functions. Shall I attempt to establish a temporary communications relay?
Once the undersea database is fully linked, the access privileges it grants will significantly amplify your communications priority.
This should assist you in reaching the outside world for support.
Cordelia let out a long breath of relief. Those were the words she had been desperate to hear.
She curled her fingers into her palm and held on tight, waiting until she was absolutely certain that this hard-won piece of good news was not a cruel illusion.
Once her heartbeat had steadied, Cordelia turned and made her way to the weather monitoring room next door.
Larsen... the comms can be brought back on—what's going on?
Larsen was hunched over the weather instruments, his eyes fixed on the readings.
Across the satellite's thermal image, a disturbing crimson stain stood out against the deep blue, clustered near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
This warm patch... it's December now... it shouldn't be...
An underwater volcano...? Or the geothermal platforms running wild after the ocean current system went down?
There's a residual tropical depression sitting right here. It should have dissipated by now. But with the ocean current system online, anomalies like this aren't exactly rare.
The problem is, this warm patch has it "trapped" in place.
Will it make the weather worse?
Worse isn't the word for it.
Larsen pointed to the polar satellite feed.
A dense, towering band of white cloud stretched across the image.
If this depression collides with that cold front... we'd be looking at a hybrid system. The kind that doesn't follow any of the normal rules.

An anomalous warm pool. An out-of-season tropical depression. Polar cold air. All of it converging on the same patch of ocean at the same time... A coincidence like this... only a god could arrange it.
...And this island won't survive a storm like that.
Though the storm had not yet arrived, the ocean wind streamed through the window and set her clothes snapping.
The baby in her arms had fallen asleep, one tiny hand clutching her collar, breathing slow and steady as if lost in a long, peaceful dream.
Alone on the vast water, Karenina stands on her surfboard, the waves carrying her up and down in a slow, endless rhythm.
If you stick to the route I marked, you should stay clear of the waters contaminated by the Red Tide.
Commandant, how's the ship holding up?
But the engines are giving out.
We've beached her on a reef for now.
It was Larsen's idea. After steadying himself from memories he can barely face, he offered a safer plan.
Got it. I'll locate a landing site and circle back for you.
The vast ocean meets an ink-black sky, and in that endless dark, a single light flickers.
It glows like the faintest glimmer of a firefly.
I think... I'm catching a light signal.
Clear of the Red Tide's densest stain, the ocean opens into a dark, limitless expanse. That single, firefly glow becomes impossible to miss.
The warm light beats on in a steady rhythm, constant as a star that refuses to stop burning in the great dark above.
Karenina studies the flickering signal, trying to decipher its pattern.
A strange familiarity washes over her, unbidden, and a sudden warmth floods her chest.
Commandant, I'm going to check it out...
It stretches into a long, thin thread, sewing her path to some unknown place ahead.
As she draws closer, a winding ribbon of light sways gently with the waves.
It's like a glowing river meandering its way home.
Huh? Wait. Don't tell me... No interest in drawing, no interest in singing, but engineering is what gets her attention?
The soft sea wraps around her, warm and familiar, the way someone once held her long ago.
Karenina follows the ribbon of light and steps onto a crumbling port.
Everywhere she looks, there is only ruin.
The buildings along the port have lost all trace of what they once were.
Her memories, separated from her by so many years, remain shrouded in fog, unclear and distant.
She remembers the dark chaos of a ship cabin, and so much blood.
Through the blurred images, there are crabs lunging with claws raised, gunfire, screaming, and a pair of arms that held everything terrible at bay.
This was the path she traveled the first time she came here.
Karenina ventures deeper inside and comes to a room whose walls are torn open with holes.
It feels as though this place has witnessed more than its share of arguments.
And I do hope that in a place like that, absolute reason can give birth to absolute compassion... Compassion for all of humanity.
A vivid red flashes through her mind, the long hair of the woman who held her, brushing against her cheek and dancing before her eyes.
Karenina remembers how she could never stop herself from reaching for it, the way one chases a flame, chasing its light and its warmth.
The spell of memory loosens, and Karenina surfaces with a long, deep breath.
Commandant, I think... this place used to be a military base...
Threaded through the fog of those old memories, she can almost hear Larsen speaking.
Larsen... he might have served here...
Karenina moves through a narrow corridor. A faded sign on the wall indicates she is about to enter the residential quarters.
Around the next corner, she sees the base's name.
This is... the Rainbow Bridge Military Base.
Between the realm of the gods and the world of men, the burning Rainbow Bridge served as the road to heaven.
During Ragnarok, the fire giants thundered across it, and the bridge shattered beneath their heavy tread. The seas boiled in the wake of its flames.
On the other end of the M.I.N.D. connection, a long silence settles in.
At the stern of the Starshadow, the moment the name of the military base passes your lips, Larsen goes utterly still.
I thought... the whole base had broken apart and sunk...
The icy seawater seems to rise around him once more. He fights for breath, chest heaving, until he slowly brings himself back under control.
If... if she's at Rainbow Bridge... then Mirage Island is close. The Lighthouse there still has the comms equipment we set up, and there should be lifeboats in the dock below...
He clutches the poetry collection to his chest and squeezes it until his knuckles go white.
If we can reach the Lighthouse... we'll have a way forward.
The Rainbow Bridge Military Base looks nothing like what Larsen remembers.
A chime from the PA system echoes through the halls, and the indicator lights in the living quarters flicker on one by one.
After a quick round of adjustments by Karenina, the ventilation and lighting systems hum back to life.
If we've got a direction, and we use this base as a reference point, it shouldn't be too hard to find.

After the base's structural collapse, all maintenance systems ceased operation. Seafloor currents and tectonic microshifts may have induced non-periodic drift in the remaining sections, affecting positional accuracy.
Navigation planning also requires dynamic adjustment based on seasonal current vectors and monsoon models.
As you relay the information on Mirage Island, Karenina hears the voice, and her grip tightens around her weapon.
I am Frigga, the central intelligence of Rainbow Bridge Military Base. It is a pleasure to assist you.
Correct. Broadcasting standard time. The current year is 216...
The central AI's voice cuts off mid-sentence.
Apologies. Background data update in progress.
Allow me to reintroduce myself. I am the backup central intelligence of Rainbow Bridge Military Base, activated only after the primary system went fully offline.
I retain all data from the primary system. For convenience, you may continue to address me as Frigga.
It seems... I have been dormant for a considerable period. Cordelia granted me an extended leave of absence.
For vacations... the longer, the better.
Is that a standard human conversational pattern? Curious. I have encountered a similar sentiment before...
So when you leave, will you also tell me... "See you later"?
"Miss Visitor" sounds too odd to her ears, so Karenina offers her name instead.
Rainbow Bridge had a small warship registered under the designation Karenin.
Karenina, I'm rather fond of your name. How may I assist you?
Frigga... What happened on the day this base sank?
I regret that within your specified time parameters, the primary system had already been corrupted by an unknown virus.
I... cannot ac... cess... detailed... re... cords...
Her voice stutters for a split second, and the blue lights pulsing through the living quarters abruptly switch to a warning yellow.
Karenina sweeps her gaze across the room, every sense on edge.
We're running out of time, Karenina.
When the base broke apart, my core program went down with the central control system. The backup instance running in the living quarters cannot sustain extended operation.
I will soon be departing on a rather extended vacation. Please proceed with haste, Karenina.
Input your available data, and I will... chart a... course for you.
Karenina doesn't hesitate. She keys in the route details drawn from Larsen's memory without a moment's pause.
Ah. The day the base came apart.
It was winter then. Now the season is summer. Some recalculation will be required.
It seems this will be the final directive I carry out.
It has been a pleasure to be of use to you, Karenina.
In the brief moments it takes for the route to generate, Karenina casts one last careful look around the living quarters, a place that feels both known and strange.
My instance is approaching termination. Before it does, Karenina, may I ask you a question?
The final directive I executed before my last dormancy was to sink the warship Balder.
When Commander Gunnar assigned me my designation, he told me that Frigga was the mother of Balder, the god of light. She once commanded all things in creation not to harm her child.
He said that as the central intelligence of Rainbow Bridge, my duty was to protect this place. The way a mother, in human terms, would protect her child.
This has caused me some confusion and some contradiction.
Karenina, I would like to know how the story ends.
Sorry, I... don't really know that myth... Hold on.
She remembers what Mara said when they first met.

The Balder's construction started way back in the Golden Age. Even settling on a name took forever. In the end, it inherited its designation from the first warship that went down in the Atlantic during the Punishing Virus outbreak.

In the old stories, the death of Balder, the god of light, was what set Ragnarok in motion. And his return brought order to the new world... Karenina, you and your people are the hope of that new world.
The death of Balder, the god of light, was what set Ragnarok in motion. And when he returned from the realm of death, he brought order to the new world...
Humans are remarkably skilled at telling stories.
Karenina, the new course has been transmitted to your terminal. I wish you all the best.
I'm going to rest now. I'll see you later.
The AI's voice remains calm and flat, so flat it barely registers as a farewell.
Karenina lingers at the small dining table in the living quarters for a while.
Finally, she gets to her feet, takes the old candlestick from the table, and walks out toward the dock.
Across the sea, the moon spills a road of silver-white light from the dock to the distant skyline.
The ruined port sees yet another candle flame trembling in a hand.
Its glow plays gently over Karenina's face as she hums, and the ancient tune weaves through the empty dock and over the hushed water.
It is the funeral dirge for the fallen souls.
It is a long-overdue farewell from the survivor who finally made her way back.
A beam of light shoots from the top of the tower, piercing the night and reaching far across the sea.
The sea breeze lifts her hair and tugs gently at the brim of her cap.

Karenina glances back at the base one last time. The light strips coil around it, their warm white glow making the surrounding waters look bright and almost welcoming, as if the sea has forgotten how to be cold.
But it is time for her to go.
